issues.legal_issue: Proof that a will was duly executed and attested does not, by itself, establish that the will is genuine or remove the court’s duty to examine suspicious circumstances.
A court may decline to act on a duly executed will when the propounder fails to dispel suspicious circumstances to the court’s satisfaction.

A first appellate court may not treat findings on due execution, testamentary capacity, forgery, or undue influence as a finding that a will is genuine without properly considering their cumulative effect and the trial court’s treatment of suspicious circumstances.
A reasoned judgment of a single judge cannot be interfered with without deep consideration.
